sections.body: Citation mapping and discovery is the practice of treating research papers as points in a network, where links are citations and shared meaning. In this section, artificial intelligence is not predicting the future in a vague way; it is computing actual citation graphs from the 135 research papers in the site library and the 11,075 claims extracted from them. The work involves measuring how often papers cite each other, how their abstracts and claims cluster by topic, and how a single paper's citation context changes over time. It also includes finding bridge studies that connect two fields that rarely cite each other, and using those patterns to forecast which research areas are gaining attention. The goal is to make the structure of the literature visible, not to replace reading the papers.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The state of this work is uneven. Citation graph construction is largely solved for standard bibliographic data, but the site's library is small at 135 papers, so any trend forecast is based on a narrow sample. Clustering papers by meaning works well when claims are clean, but the 11,075 extracted claims still contain noise from varying writing styles and incomplete extraction. How a paper is cited is harder to summarize automatically because citation context can be positive, negative, or neutral, and current models often miss that nuance. Bridge studies between fields are promising but limited by the fact that the site does not link to a search tool, only to original papers, so discovery depends on the papers already in the library. Honest limits include small sample size, possible extraction errors, and the inability to capture citations that are not in the indexed set.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages under this section move from raw structure to interpretation. Citation Graphs Over Time shows the basic network of who cites whom and how that network changes, which is the starting point for any reader. Clustering Papers by Meaning uses the extracted claims to group papers that are about the same thing even if they do not cite each other, so a reader goes there to find related work by content rather than by reference. How a Paper Is Cited zooms in on a single paper and examines the sentences around each citation, which helps a reader judge whether a paper is being supported or challenged. Bridge Studies Between Fields identifies papers that connect two otherwise separate clusters, useful for a reader looking for interdisciplinary work. Forecasting Research Trends takes the patterns from the previous four pages and projects which topics are rising or falling, but a reader should treat those projections as descriptive patterns from the 135 paper library, not as predictions of the whole field. Each page links to the original paper rather than a search tool, so a reader can verify the source directly.
